source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 8 Analysis of Competing Hypotheses
finding: ACH is an eight-step procedure: identify hypotheses; list evidence and assumptions; build a matrix and judge diagnosticity; refine and delete non-diagnostic items; draw tentative conclusions by trying to refute; test sensitivity; report all hypotheses; set milestones. Heuer says it rests on cognitive psychology, decision analysis and the scientific method.
numbers: 8 steps. Matrix: hypotheses across the top, evidence down the side. Cell marks C, I, N/A or plus/minus; double marks for strong. Advises 3 to 7 hypotheses, more than 7 should be grouped.
quote: ACH is an eight-step procedure grounded in basic insights from cognitive psychology, decision analysis, and the scientific method.
limits: Heuer says he developed it for hard problems. The chapter reports no experiment. Claims of being 'surprisingly effective, proven' are asserted, not tested.
agent_relevance: The eight steps map to an agent loop, but the cost is high. Any step kept must earn its place by a test.

source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 8 Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (steps 3 to 5: diagnosticity and counting minuses)
finding: Core logic: work across rows, one evidence item at a time, to find diagnostic items; then work down columns. The hypothesis with the fewest inconsistent cells is most likely; consistent cells (pluses) count for little because evidence that fits any reasonable hypothesis is easy to list.
numbers: Ranking rule: fewest minuses wins. Optional refinement: for each cell ask the probability of seeing this evidence if the hypothesis is true. Heuer also says the matrix should not dictate the conclusion.
quote: The hypothesis with the fewest minuses is probably the most likely one.
limits: The minus-counting rule discards confirming evidence and base rates; later studies show analysts do not follow it (see a10, a15). It is not a Bayesian rule.
agent_relevance: If a matrix step is used, code should drop rows that fit all hypotheses, and should never count only minuses without a likelihood check.

source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 8 Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (working memory claim and generation stage)
finding: Heuer's psychological rationale: holding 3 to 7 hypotheses in working memory and tracking each evidence item against each is beyond most people, so a matrix is an external memory aid. People are also poor at generating all hypotheses; he cites Gettys et al. (1980) and separates generation from evaluation. Unproven hypotheses must be kept alive until disproved (his India 1998 example: a deception hypothesis).
numbers: Cites Gettys et al. 1980 hypothesis-generation report. No numbers given for the claim.
limits: Rationale is about human working memory. An LLM holds a long list of rows in context without that limit, though it may still attend unevenly.
agent_relevance: The memory-aid argument does not carry over to an agent; the keep-rivals-alive and generate-before-evaluate parts might.

source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 8 Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (summary: what ACH claims to guarantee)
finding: Heuer states three distinguishing elements: work with a set of hypotheses rather than a favourite; find diagnostic evidence; try to refute. He says there is no guarantee of a correct answer, only an appropriate process and an audit trail. He also says expert users may absorb the concepts and drop the full eight steps.
numbers: Claims it 'increases the odds of getting the right answer'; no test cited.
quote: It increases the odds of getting the right answer, and it leaves an audit trail
limits: Process and accuracy are separated by the author himself: a good audit trail is not shown to raise accuracy.
agent_relevance: Treat the matrix as a record for others to audit, not as an accuracy booster.

source: Mandel and Tetlock (2018) Correcting judgment correctives in national security intelligence, Frontiers in Psychology 9:2640
finding: Argues that Heuer never tested ACH and that intelligence tradecraft norms rest on the 'goodness heuristic' (if a method seems good on inspection, adopt it). Quotes Heuer's 2010 reply that common sense should suffice and that he would ignore tests that did not match IC use.
numbers: Heuer reply dated 15 Aug 2010: would 'ignore it and stick with my common sense judgment' if tests did not replicate how ACH is used. Perspective article, no new data.
limits: Opinion piece with argument, not an experiment. Heuer's quote is as reported by the authors.
agent_relevance: Do not adopt a scaffold step because it sounds sensible; require a measured gain.

source: Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami (2018) Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails? JDM 13(6)
finding: First randomised test of ACH on real analysts. 50 UK analysts, about 25 per group, did a paper task: which of four tribes a target belongs to, given base rates and 12 probabilistic cues (6 present, 6 absent). ACH group got training and followed 8 steps; control chose its own approach. ACH did not improve accuracy.
numbers: N=50 (mean age 27.79, mean experience 14.08 months). Priors: Acanda 5%, Bango 20%, Conda 30%, Dengo 45%. Mean absolute error vs naive Bayes: control 0.21 [0.17,0.26], ACH 0.26 [0.22,0.29]; difference 0.04, p=.14, d=0.43 favouring control. Random guessing 0.33. Rank correlation with Bayes: ACH 0.29, control 0.24.
quote: the control group was a little more accurate (and coherent) than the ACH group
limits: Small, young sample; fully quantified task with neat hypotheses; ground truth is a naive Bayes model; ACH group may not use the method as on the job; control group was not told to avoid matrices.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a full ACH procedure does not beat plain judgment. Compare any matrix step against a no-matrix arm at equal calls.

source: Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami (2018) JDM 13(6) - coherence
finding: Probabilities of four exclusive hypotheses should sum to 1 but did not in either group. ACH was somewhat less coherent on additivity.
numbers: Sum of four probabilities: control 1.54 [1.33,1.76], ACH 1.77 [1.56,1.97], difference 0.22, p=.13, d=0.45. Binary complements: control 0.98, ACH 0.95. Additivity violation: ACH 0.82, control 0.56, p=.08, d=0.52. Quantity disagreement share of error: ACH 0.73 vs control 0.50, p=.04.
limits: Differences not significant except the last; medium effect sizes favour control.
agent_relevance: Unpacking into many hypotheses inflates totals. Normalise probabilities in code after any multi-hypothesis scoring.

source: Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami (2018) JDM 13(6) - cue usefulness
finding: ACH training made analysts rate each cue's usefulness much closer to its true probability gain, yet this did not raise final accuracy. In the control group, better usefulness ratings did go with lower error.
numbers: Correlation of rated usefulness with probability gain: ACH 0.68 [0.61,0.75], control 0.17 [-0.02,0.35], d=1.59, p<.001. Correlation of usefulness tracking with MAE: ACH r=-.10 (p=.63), control r=-.42 (p=.045), overall r=-.14.
limits: The disconnect was unexpected and the authors call for replication. Only the diagnosticity-rating part of ACH shows a gain.
agent_relevance: Diagnosticity scoring can be learned, but the score must be wired into the final answer by code, not left to the last step.

source: Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami (2018) JDM 13(6) - statistical repair
finding: What worked was not ACH but post-hoc statistics. Forcing judgments to be coherent cut error by 35%. Averaging coherentised judgments across the 50 analysts cut error 61%. Weighting by coherence did not beat equal weights.
numbers: Coherentization: MAE 0.23 to 0.15 (d=0.96; control d=0.69, ACH d=1.37). Normalisation MAE 0.13. Equal-weight pool of 50: MAE 0.09 (61% reduction). Coherence weighting beta=5 no better. Gains mostly from groups of 1 to 3; random data gave a similar variance-reduction gain.
limits: Authors credit most of the gain to averaging noise, not crowd wisdom. Task is a single quantified case.
agent_relevance: Strong support for the schema's code-side normalisation and many-draws aggregation over a judged procedure step.

source: Dhami, Belton and Mandel (2019) The 'analysis of competing hypotheses' in intelligence analysis, Applied Cognitive Psychology 33(6):1080-1090
finding: Process analysis of the same 50-analyst data. ACH-trained analysts did not follow all steps; evidence for reduced confirmation bias was mixed; ACH may raise inconsistency and error. Wilcox and Mandel (2023) add: most ACH analysts deviated from at least one step, mostly by using consistent evidence, and used base rates less than the control group.
numbers: N=50 (same data as Mandel 2018). From Wilcox and Mandel Table 2 and section 4: 20 of 25 ACH analysts used consistent evidence against instructions; 16 of 25 control analysts spontaneously built an ACH-style matrix. ACH group listed all cues correctly more often.
quote: ACH-trained analysts did not follow all of the steps of ACH.
limits: Only the abstract page was opened for this entry; the step-level counts come from the review (a14).
agent_relevance: A program would not skip steps, but the base-rate neglect risk remains: a matrix of consistent/inconsistent cells has no slot for a prior.

source: Karvetski and Mandel (2020) Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help? JDM 15(6):939-958
finding: Online experiment, 227 Canadian graduates, 6 cases in 3 isomorphic pairs, 3 evidence items and 2 hypotheses each (gang member or street artist). ACH (modelled on the PARC tool) vs no technique. No coherence gain on any test.
numbers: N=227 (Qualtrics, mean age 40.7, 26.4% male). Judgment-choice match .74 overall, method effect d=0.15, p=.25. Bayesian agreement phi .65, d=0.06. MAD from Bayes .31 raw, d=0.13. Additivity: method F=1.52, p=.22. Conservatism: Bayesian distance from 50/50 .33 vs elicited .13, d=1.54 for everyone.
quote: the ACH group showed no advantage over a no-technique control group.
limits: Only 3 items and 2 hypotheses; not real analysts; coherence only indirectly tied to accuracy; 31.7% of people had a probability clipped to .9999 or .0001.
agent_relevance: Small cases favour no matrix. A matrix may matter only with many items and hypotheses, which this test did not reach.

source: Karvetski and Mandel (2020) JDM 15(6) - reliability across isomorphic cases
finding: ACH users gave less consistent answers on structurally identical cases than controls.
numbers: Mean absolute difference between matched pairs: ACH .22 [.19,.24], control .18 [.16,.20]; F=3.86, p=.05 (.051), d=0.20.
quote: Participants who used ACH were less reliable across isomorphic cases than control participants
limits: Small, borderline effect; the authors suggest ACH is cognitively burdensome and pulls attention from natural reasoning.
agent_relevance: Test any matrix step for run-to-run consistency on paired rephrasings, not accuracy alone.

source: Karvetski and Mandel (2020) JDM 15(6) - pseudo-diagnostic weighting
finding: ACH users let evidence that fits both hypotheses move their judgment. Non-diagnostic evidence carried about a third of the weight of fully diagnostic evidence, which is the opposite of ACH's aim.
numbers: Regression of differential consistency on probability terms: slope B=0.502, SE=0.082, p<.001, R2=.055; non-diagnostic weight about 32%. Robustness check (C=1, CC=2): slope 1.20, about 30%.
quote: The ACH group also showed pseudo-diagnostic weighting of evidence.
limits: Could only be measured in the ACH group (control did not rate alternatives). The PARC scoring rule counts only I and II marks, which the authors call problematic.
agent_relevance: In any agent matrix, code must zero out rows that are equally consistent with all hypotheses.

source: Wilcox and Mandel (2023) Critical review of the Analysis of Competing Hypotheses technique, Intelligence and National Security (forthcoming; PsyArXiv an32t)
finding: Review of all experiments with an ACH arm and a no-technique control. Google Scholar search returned 244 entries; 7 articles describing 6 experiments met the rules. Verdict: ACH as a whole gives little to no benefit and may harm judgment; they discourage mandating it.
numbers: 244 hits, 7 articles, 6 experiments. Table 3: no difference in accuracy (studies 2, 4, 5); no difference in confirmation bias (1, 6, 7); detrimental on diagnosticity (4, 5), reliability (5), base-rate use (3). Only positives: confirmation bias in non-analysts (study 1) and diagnosticity ratings (2/3).
quote: ACH--as a whole--has little to no overall benefit on judgment quality, and may even harm it
limits: Not a quantitative meta-analysis; effect sizes were too different to pool. Small studies; three papers report participants did not follow instructions. Authors include the Mandel lab, so not independent of the key studies.
agent_relevance: This is the strongest basis for schema 4b. The weaker point is the gap between human samples and an agent.

source: Wilcox and Mandel (2023) - theory critique: Popper and ignoring confirming evidence
finding: Theory objections. ACH claims Popperian falsificationism, but Popper's rule was for universal claims, and Popper rejected assigning probabilities to hypotheses and coarse inconsistency scores. ACH tells analysts to ignore consistent evidence, including base rates, which Bayesian and likelihoodist philosophy would reject. 'Consistency' is never defined, so it may invite the representativeness heuristic and inside-view thinking.
numbers: Step-6 rule: relative probability set only by inconsistent evidence. 20 of 25 ACH analysts used consistent evidence against instructions (from Dhami 2019).
limits: Argument and philosophy, not experiment.
agent_relevance: Agent matrices should record likelihood ratios, not C/I marks, if used at all.

source: Lehner, Adelman, Cheikes and Brown (2008) Confirmation bias in complex analyses, IEEE Trans. SMC-A 38(3) (MITRE report 2004), as summarised in Wilcox and Mandel (2023) Table 2
finding: Oldest positive result. 24 R&D employees (5 experienced analysts in ACH, 7 in control) judged three hypotheses for the USS Iowa explosion over four rounds of evidence; ACH tutorial modelled on Folker. Bias was the link between prior confidence and later evidence ratings. ACH cut bias only for people with no analytic experience; no effect for experienced analysts.
numbers: N=24; 2x2 (method by experience). Bias measured as correlation between prior confidence and next-round evidence rating. Rating scale -2 to +2, no aggregation rule given.
limits: Read only through the review table; the MITRE PDF returned 403, so numbers are second-hand. Very small cells; the review says the study was too underpowered to judge either group.
agent_relevance: The only ACH benefit was for novices on weighting bias; shows a matrix may help weak reasoners only.

source: Karvetski, Mandel and Irwin (2020) Improving probability judgment in intelligence analysis: from structured analysis to statistical aggregation, Risk Analysis 40(5):1040-1057, via Wilcox and Mandel Table 2 row 4
finding: Second experiment: 147 Canadian online participants, 2x3 design comparing ACH with a structured Bayesian elicitation, mushroom-species task. No accuracy gain without aggregation; ACH less accurate than the Bayesian elicitation when answers were pooled; coherence worse after using ACH than before; ACH worsened double-counting of perfectly correlated cues when the correlation was salient.
numbers: N=147. No accuracy difference unaggregated; ACH worse than Bayesian elicitation at most aggregation group sizes. Coherence worse after ACH than before in the within-subject comparison.
quote: Analytic techniques such as ACH and FBT were ineffective in improving accuracy
limits: Read through the review table; the journal full text was blocked (403).
agent_relevance: Prefer a likelihood-ratio style step plus pooling over a C/I matrix.

source: Whitesmith (2020) Cognitive Bias in Intelligence Analysis: Testing the ACH Method, Edinburgh University Press; via Wilcox and Mandel (2023)
finding: Two-hour ACH training; 32 King's College London students and 7 UK intelligence community members judged a terrorist-bioweapon scenario over seven information sets in two orders. ACH did not reduce serial-position effects or confirmation bias; confirmation bias also distorted use of ACH's own scoring.
numbers: N=32 students + 7 IC members. Five criteria for bias (belief-driven diagnosticity, belief-driven credibility, belief rising on low-credibility evidence, etc.). Participants were told their final belief need not follow ACH scores.
limits: Read through the review table. How many criteria define bias was unclear; participants were not forced to follow ACH aggregation.
agent_relevance: The hand-off from matrix to final decision can itself be biased; make the aggregation code, not judgment.

source: Maegherman, Ask, Horselenberg and van Koppen (2021) Test of the Analysis of Competing Hypotheses in Legal Decision-Making, via Wilcox and Mandel (2023)
finding: 191 Dutch and Belgian law students read evidence of guilt first. A short ACH explanation did not change guilt judgments or information search. Everyone showed little to no confirmation bias. Only 38% of ACH participants said they used the matrix.
numbers: N=191. 38% compliance with the matrix. No training beyond a short explanation.
limits: A floor effect (no bias to remove) and low compliance weaken the test. Read through the review table only.
agent_relevance: If the baseline does not show the bias, a debiasing structure has nothing to fix.

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva and Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation, Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications 9:37 - Study 1
finding: Study 1: UK students saw 3 two-hypothesis, 12-evidence tasks as text, as an ACH matrix (hypotheses in columns) or as a matrix with hypotheses in rows. Only the hypotheses-in-rows layout cut the confirmation-bias strategy. The standard ACH layout did not.
numbers: N=161 (mean age 20.0, 90.1% female). Task 1 chose the confirming option in 56.5% overall. Layout vs strategy chi2(2)=9.43, p=.009, phi=.24. Hypotheses-in-rows less likely to choose the confirming option (p=.003); columns p=.327; text p=.048. Evidence-credibility sensitivity 77% columns, 78% rows, 75% text; chi2(2)=0.15, p=.927.
quote: individuals presented with hypotheses in rows and evidence items in columns were significantly less likely to demonstrate confirmation bias
limits: Student volunteers; bias indexed by one forced choice. Power calculation: 141 needed for a medium effect at .90 power.
agent_relevance: Layout of the evidence table in a prompt is a cheap A/B test: options as rows.

source: Dhami et al. (2024) Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications 9:37 - Study 2 (62 Dutch military analysts)
finding: Study 2: most real analysts did not show confirmation bias. Analysts using a balanced strategy were almost all sensitive to evidence credibility. Neither coherence nor cognitive reflection predicted better performance.
numbers: N=62. Strategy: 19.4% confirming-only, 14.5% disconfirming-only, 66.1% balanced. 83.3% switched hypothesis when source credibility dropped (excluding one). By strategy: 98% of balanced, 72.7% of confirming, 33.3% of disconfirming were credibility-sensitive. CRT mean 2.32 (SD 0.92); mean absolute deviation from additivity 15.42.
quote: the majority of 62 Dutch military analysts did not suffer from confirmation bias
limits: Single scenario type; military analysts, not a random IC sample.
agent_relevance: Real expert users may not need the debiasing tool; the bias it targets may be rarer than assumed.

source: Karvetski and Mandel (2020) JDM 15(6) - why ACH may add error
finding: The authors give reasons ACH may add error: it is cognitively burdensome, it pulls attention away from natural problem-specific reasoning, and it may hurt competent reasoners while helping weak ones. The last point is a hypothesis awaiting test (also repeated by Wilcox and Mandel section 4.1.3).
numbers: No numbers for the explanation.
limits: Mechanism is conjecture.
agent_relevance: Matrix scaffolds may help weak models and hurt strong ones; test by model strength, as HypoArena shows model-dependent shifts (a27).

source: Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami (2018) - limitations as stated
finding: Authors list limits: small homogeneous sample, neat quantified task without real-world messiness, ground truth from a naive Bayes model with conditional independence, ACH group may not mirror field use, and the disconnect between cue rating and accuracy needs replication.
numbers: Medium effect sizes (d around 0.43 to 0.52) all favour control but p>.05.
limits: Underpowered for medium effects: a true small harm or small gain could both hide.
agent_relevance: Boundary: no test yet on open, many-hypothesis, messy tasks, so the null is for small clean tasks.

source: Cheikes et al. (2004) MITRE report 04-0985 Confirmation bias in complex analyses; search snippet only
finding: Search summary says the goals were to replicate Tolcott-style confirmation bias in complex analysis and test whether ACH reduces it; ACH reduced bias only among participants without analytic experience, and the bias appeared as weighting rather than interpretation.
numbers: Not read; PDF blocked.
limits: Snippet only; numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: Check the full report before citing weighting-versus-interpretation.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) AgentCDM: Enhancing multi-agent collaborative decision-making via ACH-inspired structured reasoning, arXiv 2508.11995
finding: A multi-agent LLM framework taking ACH as inspiration: agents move from passive answer selection or voting to evaluating and building hypotheses. Two-stage training: first with explicit ACH-style scaffolding, then with the scaffolding removed. Claims state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks.
numbers: The abstract gives no numbers or baseline names. Not an ablation of ACH versus no ACH.
limits: Abstract only; training is involved, so any gain mixes ACH structure with fine-tuning. No equal-compute no-ACH control is stated in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Scaffold removal in stage 2 hints the structure is a training aid and not an inference-time need, but this is unproven.

source: Marozzo and Lio (2026) LLM-as-an-Investigator: evidence-first agentic reasoning for robust interactive problem diagnosis, arXiv 2606.13220
finding: An agent with a Hypothesis Investigator that keeps competing hypotheses, a Counterfactual Investigator that challenges the current explanation, and cited-evidence records. Tested on 303 technical forum threads in 3 domains against direct, reasoning, ReAct and Tree-of-Thoughts baselines.
numbers: 303 threads (mechanical, electrical, hydraulic). The abstract reports no numeric results.
limits: Abstract only; ablations exist but no figures were read. It is ACH-like, not ACH.
agent_relevance: Closest agent analogue to a rivals-plus-evidence record; measure whether the counterfactual challenger is the active ingredient.

source: HypoArena (2026) Before the Action: Benchmarking LLMs on Prospective Hypothesis Discovery, arXiv 2607.15766 - ACH as an agent skill
finding: 15 LLMs on 988 cases in 6 domains, baseline single pass vs agent mode where the model can pick from 12 structured analytic skills adapted from intelligence methods, including ACH. Skills gave no uniform gain.
numbers: 988 cases, 15 models, judge seed-2.0-pro with pairwise Bradley-Terry ratings. Agent-minus-baseline shifts range from +88 (kimi-k2.5) to about -60 (claude-opus-4.6). Correlation of shift with baseline strength: Spearman rho = -0.10. Judge vs human experts on 1,500 pairs: Kendall tau .90, Spearman .98. Failure mode noted: candidate compression.
quote: Agent mode does not provide uniform gains.
limits: Measures hypothesis-set quality judged by an LLM, not truth accuracy. ACH is bundled with 11 other skills, so its own effect is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Model-dependent, not clearly positive: the same scaffold helped some models and hurt a top one.

source: HypoArena (2026) - how the ACH skill is specified
finding: The ACH skill in the benchmark library uses an evidence-diagnosticity matrix with C/I/NA scoring, ranks hypotheses by inconsistency (least disconfirming evidence wins) and is meant to guard against confirmation bias. It uses Heuer's rule unchanged, including the counting of minuses.
numbers: One of 12 skills (others include Structured Brainstorming, Chronology, Assumptions Check). Appendix K, Table 14.
limits: Describes the prompt, not an effect.
agent_relevance: Benchmark authors use the Heuer rule, which human studies suggest is the weak part; LLM tests of a likelihood-ratio variant are missing.

source: Wilcox and Mandel (2023) - gaps in the ACH literature
finding: The review implies several untested points: no test splits ACH into parts (hypothesis listing, matrix, scoring rule, ignore-confirming rule); the matrix-preference and diagnosticity benefits are not replicated; no test with many hypotheses or messy real cases. None of the 7 studies has an LLM arm.
numbers: Seven studies in Table 3; none with an LLM arm. The review recommends decomposition studies.
limits: The LLM-gap statement is my reading plus my own limited search (arXiv and OpenAlex APIs were rate-limited; 2 web searches used), so LLM coverage may be incomplete.
agent_relevance: Our own bench could give the first controlled agent test: matrix vs no matrix at equal calls.

source: Wilcox and Mandel (2023) - where ACH might not go wrong
finding: Possible useful parts: externalising the evidence list and the matrix layout. In one study 16 of 25 control analysts built an ACH-style matrix unprompted; in another the matrix got a mean usefulness rating of 57.1 (SD 18.8) out of 100, although 62% of the ACH group said they did not use it.
numbers: 16/25 spontaneous matrices (Dhami 2019 data); usefulness 57.1 (SD 18.8); 62% did not use the matrix. None replicated.
limits: Control analysts had earlier been told to use matrices, so spontaneity is doubtful.
agent_relevance: Keep as a hypothesis: listing evidence against every rival may help, but only in layout form, rivals as rows (a20).
